title: Second complete map of a fruit fly brain completed
gist: A four-year collaboration between HHMI's Janelia Research Campus and Google mapped every neuron and roughly 300 million synapses in a male fruit fly brain using generative and recurrent AI models, completing a matched pair with an earlier female connectome and revealing specific neural circuitry behind sex-linked behavioral differences.

insights.claim: Researchers completed a full connectome—a map of every neuron and its synaptic connections—for a male fruit fly brain, joining an earlier connectome of a female fly completed earlier this year.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Provides the second-ever complete brain connectome and the first matched male/female pair, a new baseline tool for neurobiology research.
insights.locator: On Friday, researchers announced the completion of a map

insights.claim: The project was a collaboration between biologists at HHMI's Janelia Research Campus and computer scientists at Google, with both groups stating neither could have completed it alone.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Illustrates that frontier neuroscience infrastructure now requires combined biology and large-scale AI/ML engineering capability, not either alone.
insights.locator: The new work involved a collaboration between biologists

insights.claim: Although the fruit fly nervous system has only roughly 150,000 neurons, the new work identified more than 300 million synaptic connections in the fly brain alone, since each neuron can branch into hundreds of connections to others.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Quantifies the combinatorial complexity that made manual mapping infeasible and necessitated AI-assisted reconstruction.
insights.locator: the new work discovered over 300 million synaptic connections

insights.claim: The entire process took roughly four years to go from an intact dissected fly brain to a finished connectome, using a team of about 50 people.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete cost/time benchmark against which future, more complex connectome projects (e.g., mouse) will be measured.
insights.locator: All of this took roughly four years

themes.theme: AI methods that made the mapping possible

insights.claim: Gerry Rubin recalled that in the early 1970s researchers tried to use then-available computers to assemble the connectome of C. elegans, a worm with just over 300 neurons, but found the computers 'nowhere near powerful enough' and resorted to tracing photographic prints by hand.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Shows just how far compute and AI capability have advanced relative to the scale of the connectomics problem over roughly five decades.
insights.quote: It took them about two years to realize that the computers were nowhere near powerful enough,
insights.locator: Gerry Rubin, a senior group leader at the Janelia Research Campus

insights.claim: The team physically sliced a dissected fruit fly brain into a large series of evenly spaced sections and imaged them with electron microscopy at resolution fine enough to identify small cellular structures, then used computers to reconstruct the 3D architecture.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Describes the physical-to-digital pipeline underlying modern connectomics, a repeatable process for other species.
insights.locator: the biologists took a dissected fruit fly brain

insights.claim: Google's Michal Januszewski said a generative AI model is first used to digitally smooth over the physical gaps and distortions introduced when brain tissue is sliced and imaged, making all downstream processing easier.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A concrete example of generative AI solving a physical-data-quality problem rather than a text or image generation task, showing AI's expanding role in scientific instrumentation.
insights.quote: We use [a generative] model to make the tissue look as if the seams were not there, and that then makes all the downstream processing easier because you can basically ignore the problem to a large degree.
insights.locator: Michal Januszewski, a staff scientist at Google Research

insights.claim: A separate recurrent AI model fills in cell membrane boundaries to track individual neurons across 3D space, converting microscope image voxels into a 3D neuron reconstruction—a process Januszewski said 'literally moves through space' as it builds each neuron's outline, unlike typical conceptions of AI.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Highlights a distinct, spatially-recurrent AI architecture purpose-built for volumetric biological reconstruction, relevant beyond neuroscience to any 3D imaging domain.
insights.quote: it is actually a recurrent process, so it literally moves through space as it makes the outline of the neurons, and it is a visual model
insights.locator: "It is different in a number of ways from what people commonly think

insights.claim: Additional AI models recognize and classify synapses, with their sensitivity iteratively tuned through feedback from human proofreaders, since Rubin said it is 'harder to disassemble than it is to assemble' erroneous connections.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Shows the final system is a human-AI feedback loop rather than a fully automated pipeline, relevant to how much labor connectomics still requires at scale.
insights.quote: This has to be tuned by going back and forth between the proofreaders and Mikhail
insights.locator: These models can be fine-tuned using different levels of sensitivity

insights.claim: Rubin said the goal is for the tools developed on the fly project to let a future mouse connectome—despite having a thousand times more neurons—still be completed by a similarly sized team of about 50 people, since 'the people will not need to scale with the number of neurons.'
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Implies AI-driven automation could decouple connectomics labor cost from brain complexity, a key economic threshold for scaling to more complex organisms.
insights.quote: The hope is, by the time someone does a mouse, they’ll also need a team of 50 people, even though there are a thousand times more neurons in there.
insights.locator: "Our view is we did Drosophila with a team of 50 people,"

insights.claim: Google's Januszewski described the fly connectome as 'this type of grand challenge that just cannot be done in any other way,' saying it required AI because it could not be solved with more human labor or any other existing technology.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Frames the project as a genuine proof point for AI enabling scientific work that was previously fundamentally intractable, not merely faster.
insights.quote: We knew we need AI for this. This cannot be solved by having more humans or by any other technology. And it’s important.
insights.locator: "The reason I think Google and we were interested

insights.claim: Comparing the male and female fly connectomes, researchers identified 289 male-specific neurons, 71 female-specific neurons, and 138 neurons present in both sexes but with different shapes and connections.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Provides the first precise neuron-level census of sex-linked brain wiring differences in any species' complete connectome.

insights.claim: Ninety percent of male-specific neurons expressed the sex-determination genes doublesex and fruitless, but the remaining 10 percent did not, and nearly 40 percent of shared-but-differently-shaped neurons lacked active dsx or fru expression—showing gene activity and physical sex differences do not always align directly.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Complicates the simple genetic model of sex determination, suggesting some neurons acquire sex-specific identity indirectly through network interactions rather than direct gene expression.
insights.locator: Ninety percent of the male-specific neurons were making dsx and fru

insights.claim: Sex-specific neurons tend to act in higher-level integrative and decision-making brain regions rather than in immediate sensory processing or motor control, and they tend to cluster together, suggesting they act in concert to amplify behaviorally relevant signals.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Offers a generalizable structural principle for where and how sex differences are encoded in a nervous system, potentially informative beyond flies.
insights.locator: The research team also identified a general pattern

insights.claim: One connectome finding showed a specific neuron present in only one of the two brain hemispheres in the male, presumably due to a developmental glitch—though with only two connectomes complete, it is impossible to know how common such asymmetries are.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Flags an open question about individual neural variability that will require many more connectomes to resolve statistically.
insights.locator: a specific neuron seen in the female connectome was absent

themes.theme: Implications for neuroscience and future connectomics

insights.claim: Gerry Rubin said the connectome has already transformed theoretical neuroscience by giving researchers an actual wiring diagram to test hypotheses against, rather than theorizing about brain function with no structural constraints.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Suggests the connectome's biggest immediate impact is reshaping how neuroscientists formulate and test theories, not just cataloging anatomy.
insights.quote: Once they had the connectome, they could say, ‘The brain does this and here’s the wiring diagram. How can this wiring diagram allow this function?’
insights.locator: Rubin also suggested it's having a big impact on theoretical neuroscience

insights.claim: Future progress in connectomics will depend on whether costs fall the way they did in genomics as techniques are refined and automated, since building statistically meaningful sets of connectomes to study neural variability will require far faster methods than the four years the fly project took.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Frames the cost trajectory of connectomics as the key variable determining how quickly this becomes a routine research tool versus a rare, expensive undertaking.
insights.locator: Other work will depend on whether completing connectomes follows the trajectory seen in genomics
